title: The Battle of Kupres, 1992
sources: Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. I, Chapter on the Kupres operation, April 1992
ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T), context on western Bosnia 1992
Burg & Shoup, The War in Bosnia-Herzegovina (1999), Chapter 4 on early-war operations
content:
Kupres is a high plateau town in southwestern Bosnia, sitting at roughly twelve hundred metres above sea level on the watershed between the Adriatic and Black Sea drainages. The plateau itself, a broad rolling expanse of upland pasture and scattered woodland, was — and remains — a strategic position controlling the road that runs east from the Croatian coast through Tomislavgrad and then bifurcates toward Bugojno and Donji Vakuf in central Bosnia. The April 1992 battle for control of Kupres was the first significant set-piece engagement of the war between Croatian-aligned forces and the JNA-supported Serb formations in western Bosnia, and its outcome shaped the operational geometry of the subsequent campaign in the region.

The pre-war demography of Kupres municipality was mixed: roughly evenly divided among Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs, with the Serb plurality concentrated in the surrounding villages and the urban population more mixed. As the wider Yugoslav crisis intensified through late 1991 and into early 1992, local Serb authorities in Kupres aligned with the broader Bosnian Serb political project and began to organise armed formations under the patronage of JNA units stationed in the region. Local Croat authorities, in coordination with HVO formations forming in Tomislavgrad and Livno, did the same on the opposite alignment.

The battle began on 3 April 1992 when HVO and Croatian Army (HV) units crossed the watershed and advanced onto the plateau in a coordinated attack on the town and surrounding Serb-held villages. The attacking force comprised several thousand troops with armour and artillery support, and made initial progress against Serb Territorial Defence and JNA units that were thinly deployed across the plateau's broad expanse. By 5 April, Croat forces had reached the outskirts of Kupres town and engaged in fighting for the urban area itself.

The Bosnian Serb response, supported by JNA reinforcements from the Banja Luka and Knin garrisons, was substantial. Armour and artillery were committed to a counterattack that began on 7 April and continued for the next three days. The plateau's open terrain, which had assisted the Croat advance, now favoured the Serb counter-attack: open ground gave fields of fire to tanks and self-propelled guns, while the Croat formations, lacking adequate armour and air defence, found their forward positions exposed. By 10 April, the Croat units had been pushed off the plateau back across the watershed toward Tomislavgrad. The town and the broader plateau remained under Bosnian Serb control for the remainder of the year and indeed for much of the war.

Casualties on both sides were significant. Estimates from contemporaneous accounts and subsequent reconstructions place HVO and HV combat losses in the low hundreds, with comparable Bosnian Serb and JNA losses. The civilian population of the plateau, particularly Croats from the villages on the western slopes and Serbs from the villages on the eastern slopes, was displaced in significant numbers as the front line moved across their homes. The pattern of displacement was not symmetrical: Croat civilians who fled west toward Tomislavgrad as the Serb counterattack succeeded did so under conditions of rapid retreat, while Serb civilians who had been evacuated from the plateau ahead of the Croat advance returned to find their homes damaged or destroyed.

The operational significance of the Kupres battle extended beyond its local result. The defeat established that HVO and HV operations into Bosnian Serb-held territory could not be sustained against committed JNA support, even in terrain that initially favoured the attacker. The battle also demonstrated the operational alignment of the JNA, in the weeks immediately preceding the formal announcement of its withdrawal from Bosnia, with Bosnian Serb military formations: the units that conducted the counterattack on Kupres were predominantly JNA, and their commitment to the operation prefigured the seamless transfer of personnel, equipment, and command structures that would produce the VRS in mid-May.

Kupres would change hands again in late 1994, when HVO units in cooperation with elements of the ARBiH conducted a successful offensive that recaptured the plateau. By that point, the war's broader military situation had shifted substantially. The 1992 battle, however, occupies an important place in the operational record of the war's first weeks: a set-piece engagement whose outcome shaped the geography of western Bosnia for the next two and a half years.
